notes.front: What is a fixed-rate mortgage?
notes.back: A mortgage whose interest rate and monthly principal-and-interest payment stay the same for the life of the loan.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau handbook uses it as the baseline against which adjustable-rate loans are compared.
notes.example: Like a 30-year loan at 6.25% whose principal-and-interest payment is the same in year 1 and year 30, even though taxes and insurance paid alongside it may change.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 2. What is an ARM?, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: with a fixed-rate mortgage, the interest rate and the monthly payment of principal and interest stay the same during the life of the loan.

notes.front: What is an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM)?
notes.back: A mortgage whose interest rate changes periodically, usually in relation to an index, so payments may go up or down.
notes.explanation: This is the handbook's main contrast with a fixed-rate mortgage, whose rate and payment stay the same.
notes.example: Like a loan that starts at 5.5% and is reset each year to the current market rate, so the payment in year 3 may be higher or lower than in year 1.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 2. What is an ARM?, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: With an ARM, the interest rate changes periodically, usually in relation to an index, and payments may go up or down accordingly.

notes.front: In an ARM, what is the index?
notes.back: A measure of interest rates generally, on which the ARM's rate is based.
notes.explanation: An ARM's rate has two parts, the index and the margin; the index is the part that moves with the market.
notes.example: Like a published benchmark rate of 4.1% this month and 4.4% next month: the lender does not set it, it simply reads it.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.3 The index, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: The interest rate on an ARM is made up of two parts: the index and the margin. The index is a measure of interest rates generally

notes.front: In an ARM, what is the margin?
notes.back: The percentage points the lender adds to the index rate to set the ARM's interest rate.
notes.explanation: The index moves with the market; the margin is the lender's own add-on.
notes.example: Like a shop that prices goods at wholesale cost plus a fixed mark-up: here the "cost" is the index and the mark-up is the margin.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.4 The margin, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: To set the interest rate on an ARM, lenders add a few percentage points to the index rate, called the margin.

notes.front: What is the fully indexed rate of an ARM?
notes.back: The index plus the margin.
notes.explanation: It is the rate the loan would carry if no discount or cap held it down.
notes.example: Like adding a 2.5-point margin to a 3.9% index to get 6.4%, whatever lower rate the lender advertises for the first year.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.4 The margin, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: The fully indexed rate is equal to the margin plus the index.

notes.front: What is an interest-rate cap (rate cap) on an ARM?
notes.back: A limit on how much the ARM's interest rate can increase.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes two versions: a periodic adjustment cap and a lifetime cap.
notes.example: Like a speed limiter on a car: the index can race ahead, but the rate on the loan is not allowed to go past the set limit.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.5 Interest-rate caps, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: An interest-rate cap places a limit on the amount your interest rate can increase.

notes.front: What is a payment cap on an ARM?
notes.back: A limit on how much the monthly payment may increase at each adjustment.
notes.explanation: Unlike a rate cap, it limits the payment, not the interest rate.
notes.example: Like a landlord who may raise rent by no more than 5% a year, whatever happens to the landlord's own costs.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.6 Payment caps, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: limit, or cap, the amount your monthly payment may increase at the time of each adjustment.

notes.front: What is negative amortization (negative amortisation)?
notes.back: When the amount owed increases even though every required payment is made on time.
notes.explanation: It happens when payments do not cover all the interest due, so the unpaid interest is added to the balance.
notes.example: Like paying $500 a month on a card that charges $600 a month in interest: you never miss a payment, yet the balance grows.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.3 Negative amortization, PDF p. 27
notes.evidence: Negative amortization means that the amount you owe increases even when you make all your required payments on time.

notes.front: What is a hybrid ARM?
notes.back: An ARM that mixes a fixed-rate period followed by an adjustable-rate period.
notes.explanation: The rate is fixed for the first few years, then may adjust, for example annually.
notes.example: Like a phone plan with a fixed price for the first two years that then moves to whatever the current tariff is.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.1 Hybrid ARMs, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: These loans are a mix— or a hybrid—of a fixed-rate period and an adjustable-rate period.

notes.front: What is an interest-only mortgage?
notes.back: A loan that lets the borrower pay only the interest for a set number of years, typically three to ten.
notes.explanation: Payments are smaller during that period because no principal is being repaid.
notes.example: Like renting money: for the first years you pay only the charge for using it, and the amount borrowed does not shrink.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.2 Interest-only ARMs, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: An interest-only (I-O) ARM payment plan allows you to pay only the interest for a specified number of years, typically for three to 10 years.

notes.front: What is a balloon payment on a mortgage?
notes.back: A large, one-time payment due at the end of the loan term.
notes.explanation: The earlier payments do not fully pay off the loan, so the rest falls due at once.
notes.example: Like a seven-year loan with modest monthly payments and then one final bill for most of the amount borrowed.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a balloon payment? When is one allowed?
notes.evidence: A balloon payment on a mortgage is a large, one-time payment at the end of the loan term.

notes.front: Under the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act's definitions, what is a nontraditional mortgage product?
notes.back: Any mortgage product other than a 30-year fixed rate mortgage.
notes.explanation: The statute defines it by what it is not, so the category is very wide.
notes.example: Like a restaurant that calls everything except its set menu "à la carte": one standard item, and everything else falls in the other group.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. 5102 (SAFE Act definitions), § 5102(7)
notes.evidence: The term "nontraditional mortgage product" means any mortgage product other than a 30-year fixed rate mortgage.
uses: Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act

notes.front: What is a non-qualified mortgage (non-QM)?
notes.back: A loan covered by the ability-to-repay rule that does not meet any qualified mortgage definition.
notes.explanation: Such a loan does not get the presumption of compliance with the ability-to-repay requirements that a qualified mortgage gets.
notes.example: Like a car that passes the road-safety test but not the "green" standard: still legal to sell, just without the badge and what the badge brings.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.1.1, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: The consumer could attempt to show that the loan is not a QM, and therefore is not presumed to comply with the ATR requirements.

notes.front: What is a conforming loan?
notes.back: A mortgage whose original principal balance does not exceed the annual conforming loan limit for the secondary market.
notes.explanation: The Homeowners Protection Act refers to the annual conforming loan limit for the secondary market established under 12 U.S.C. 1454(a)(2).
notes.example: Like luggage that fits the airline's size limit: a loan at or under the limit fits; one over it does not.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. chapter 49 (Homeowners Protection Act)
notes.evidence: with an original principal balance that does not exceed the applicable annual conforming loan limit for the secondary market established pursuant to section 1454(a)(2) of this title

notes.front: What is a government-sponsored enterprise (GSE) in mortgage lending?
notes.back: Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, which buy or guarantee mortgage loans; the Bureau's guide describes them as operating under federal conservatorship.
notes.explanation: The ability-to-repay rules once used eligibility for GSE purchase or guarantee to define a temporary kind of qualified mortgage.
notes.example: Like a wholesaler that buys goods from many small shops so the shops can restock: lenders sell loans on and lend again.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.5.1, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: Additionally, a loan must be eligible for purchase or guarantee by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac while operating under federal conservatorship.

notes.front: What is a "jumbo" loan under Regulation Z?
notes.back: A loan whose principal balance exceeds the maximum principal obligation eligible for purchase by Freddie Mac.
notes.explanation: The Federal Housing Finance Agency sets and adjusts that maximum under federal law.
notes.example: Like a parcel too heavy for the standard postal service: it still ships, but by a different service with different rules.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.35 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, comment 35(a)(1)-3
notes.evidence: when the principal balance exceeds the limit in effect as of the date the transaction's rate is set for the maximum principal obligation eligible for purchase by Freddie Mac (a “jumbo” loan)

notes.front: What is the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) in mortgage lending?
notes.back: The federal body that insures mortgage loans; a loan it insures is an "FHA" loan.
notes.explanation: On the Loan Estimate, a loan insured by the FHA is disclosed as loan type "FHA".
notes.example: Like a guarantor on a flat lease: the landlord (lender) is protected if the tenant (borrower) stops paying.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.37 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.37(a)(11)(ii)
notes.evidence: If the loan is insured by the Federal Housing Administration, the creditor shall disclose that the loan is an “FHA.”

notes.front: What is a mortgage insurance premium (MIP), as on an FHA-insured loan?
notes.back: A premium the borrower pays for mortgage insurance; on an FHA loan it is included in the finance charge.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z's example is a $2,000 premium on an FHA-insured loan, counted in the finance charge but not in points and fees.
notes.example: Like buying travel insurance that protects the airline rather than you: you pay the premium, the other party is covered.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.32 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, comment 32(b)(1)(i)(C)
notes.evidence: if a consumer is required to pay a $2,000 mortgage insurance premium for a loan insured by the Federal Housing Administration, the $2,000 must be included in the finance charge but is not counted in points and fees.

notes.front: What is a VA home loan?
notes.back: A loan partly guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans, service members and certain surviving spouses.
notes.explanation: The VA guaranty acts as government backing for a portion of the loan.
notes.example: Like a parent who co-signs part of a child's loan: the lender has a backer for part of the risk.
notes.source: VA, Purchase and Cash-Out Refinance Home Loans, About the VA Home Loan Guaranty
notes.evidence: The VA Home Loan Guaranty program assists eligible Veterans, Servicemembers, and certain surviving spouses obtain, retain, and adapt homes.

notes.front: What is a USDA loan?
notes.back: A loan programme through the U.S. Department of Agriculture offering zero down payment to eligible borrowers in rural areas.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit lists it with FHA and VA loans as a low down payment option.
notes.example: Like a first-home scheme open only to buyers in qualifying country areas, not in the city.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 4. Choose the right down payment for you, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: USDA, which offers a similar zero down payment program for eligible borrowers in rural areas

notes.front: What is a Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM)?
notes.back: The kind of mortgage also frequently called a reverse mortgage.
notes.explanation: Regulation X names it as a type of federally related mortgage loan and treats payments to the borrower as part of servicing.
notes.example: Like an ordinary mortgage run backwards: the money flows from the lender to the homeowner.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Federally related mortgage loan"
notes.evidence: home equity conversion mortgage, also frequently called a “reverse mortgage,”

notes.front: What is a home equity line of credit (HELOC)?
notes.back: A way for a homeowner to borrow against the value of the home, for example to remodel.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit presents it as one way to borrow against home value, alongside refinancing.
notes.example: Like a credit card whose limit is set by the equity in your house, which you draw on as a kitchen project needs cash.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 4. Understand Home Equity Lines of Credit (HELOCs) and refinancing, PDF p. 27
notes.evidence: Homeowners sometimes decide they want to borrow against the value of their home to help remodel or pay for other large expenses. One way to do this is with a Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC).

notes.front: What is a construction loan?
notes.back: Usually a short-term loan that provides funds to cover the cost of building or rehabilitating a home.
notes.explanation: Its funds are typically advanced in stages as the work progresses.
notes.example: Like paying a builder in stages as the foundations, frame and roof are done, rather than all at once.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a construction loan?
notes.evidence: A construction loan is usually a short-term loan that provides funds to cover the cost of building or rehabilitating a home.

notes.front: In Regulation X's definition of "lender", how is the lien connected to the lender?
notes.back: The lender is, generally, the secured creditor named in the debt obligation and in the document creating the lien.
notes.explanation: So the lien is the security the lender holds, set out in the document that creates it.
notes.example: Like a pawnbroker's ticket that ties a loan to the watch left behind: here the home secures the debt and the lien document records it.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Lender"
notes.evidence: Lender means, generally, the secured creditor or creditors named in the debt obligation and document creating the lien.

notes.front: What is a subordinate lien, as Regulation Z uses the term?
notes.back: A lien that is not the first lien on the property, such as a second mortgage.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z sets separate higher-priced mortgage loan thresholds for first-lien and subordinate-lien loans.
notes.example: Like a second person in a queue for the same asset: if the property is sold, the first lien is paid before this one.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.35 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.35(a)(1)(iii)
notes.evidence: By 3.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a subordinate lien.

notes.front: What is table funding?
notes.back: A settlement at which the loan is funded by a contemporaneous advance of funds and assigned to the person advancing them.
notes.explanation: The person who closes the loan is not the one whose money funds it.
notes.example: Like a broker who signs the deal in its own name at the closing table while an investor hands over the cash and takes the loan at once.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Table funding"
notes.evidence: Table funding means a settlement at which a loan is funded by a contemporaneous advance of loan funds and an assignment of the loan to the person advancing the funds.

notes.front: What are discount points on a mortgage?
notes.back: Upfront charges paid at closing that lower the interest rate.
notes.explanation: They trade more cash at closing for a lower rate over time.
notes.example: Like paying a larger deposit on a phone to get a lower monthly tariff.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: Points are also called discount points. Points lower your interest rate, in exchange for paying more at closing.

notes.front: What is a lender credit on a mortgage?
notes.back: Money from the lender that lowers closing costs up front in exchange for a higher interest rate.
notes.explanation: It works like discount points in reverse.
notes.example: Like accepting a higher monthly tariff so that the phone itself costs nothing today.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: Lender credits lower your closing costs up front, in exchange for a higher interest rate.

notes.front: What is the loan-to-value ratio (LTV)?
notes.back: A measure comparing the amount financed with the appraised value of the property.
notes.explanation: The larger the down payment, the lower the LTV.
notes.example: Like borrowing $270,000 on a home appraised at $300,000: the loan is 90% of the value.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a loan-to-value ratio and how does it relate to my costs?
notes.evidence: The loan-to-value (LTV) ratio is a measure comparing the amount you are financing with the appraised value of the property.

notes.front: What is an assumable loan?
notes.back: A loan that a later buyer of the property may be permitted to take over on its original terms.
notes.explanation: The Loan Estimate must say whether this is allowed, under the label "Assumption".
notes.example: Like taking over a friend's gym membership at the old price instead of joining at today's price.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.37 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.37(m)(2)
notes.evidence: A statement of whether a subsequent purchaser of the property may be permitted to assume the remaining loan obligation on its original terms, labeled “Assumption.”

notes.front: How do lenders generally price the initial interest rate on an ARM compared with a fixed-rate mortgage?
notes.back: Lower: lenders generally charge lower initial rates for ARMs.
notes.explanation: The handbook says this makes the ARM easier on the borrower's pocket at first, against the risk of later increases.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 2. What is an ARM?, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Lenders generally charge lower initial interest rates for ARMs than for fixed-rate mortgages.

notes.front: The period between rate changes on an ARM is called the {{c1::adjustment period}}.
notes.explanation: Depending on the loan, the rate and payment may change every month, quarter, year, three years or five years.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.2 The adjustment period, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: The period between rate changes is called the adjustment period.

notes.front: If an ARM's index rate rises, what usually happens to the borrower's rate?
notes.back: It also goes up in most circumstances, and the monthly payment probably rises.
notes.explanation: The handbook hedges this: caps can limit the change, and not all ARMs adjust downward when the index falls.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.3 The index, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: If the index rate moves up, your interest rate will also go up in most circumstances, and you will probably have to make higher monthly payments.

notes.front: Does an ARM's margin usually change over the life of the loan?
notes.back: No. It may differ between lenders but usually stays the same over the life of the loan.
notes.explanation: It is the index, not the margin, that normally moves the rate after closing.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.4 The margin, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: The amount of the margin may diﬀer from one lender to another, but it usually stays the same over the life of the loan.

notes.front: What are discounted, start or teaser rates on an ARM?
notes.back: Initial rates set below the lender's fully indexed rate (index plus margin).
notes.explanation: The handbook says they are often combined with large initial fees and higher rates after the discount ends.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.1 Discounted interest rates, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: Some lenders oﬀer an ARM with an initial rate that is lower than their fully indexed ARM rate (that is, lower than the sum of the index plus the margin).

notes.front: For ability-to-repay purposes, which ARM rate must the lender generally consider, the teaser rate or the indexed rate?
notes.back: The fully indexed rate, not only the low initial rate.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that borrowers should still check that they can afford the future payments themselves.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.2 Payment shock, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: While your lender generally needs to consider this indexed rate in determining your ability to repay the loan

notes.front: What does a periodic adjustment cap on an ARM limit?
notes.back: How far the rate can move, up or down, from one adjustment period to the next after the first adjustment.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two versions of interest-rate cap in the handbook; the other covers the whole life of the loan.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.5 Interest-rate caps, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: A periodic adjustment cap, which limits the amount the interest rate can adjust up or down from one adjustment period to the next after the first adjustment

notes.front: What does a lifetime cap on an ARM limit, and how common is it?
notes.back: The rate increase over the life of the loan; by law virtually all ARMs must have one.
notes.explanation: It is the second version of interest-rate cap, alongside the periodic adjustment cap.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.5 Interest-rate caps, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: A lifetime cap, which limits the interest-rate increase over the life of the loan. By law, virtually all ARMs must have a lifetime cap.

notes.front: Can an ARM allow a bigger rate change at the first adjustment than at later ones?
notes.back: Yes. Some ARMs allow a larger change at the first adjustment, then apply a periodic cap to all later adjustments.
notes.explanation: This is why the first adjustment can be treated separately from the periodic cap.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.5.1 Periodic adjustment caps, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Some ARMs allow a larger rate change at the first adjustment and then apply a periodic adjustment cap to all future adjustments.

notes.front: An index increase not imposed because of a rate cap may be added at a later adjustment. This is called {{c1::carryover}}.
notes.explanation: So a payment can rise at an adjustment even when the index has stayed the same or fallen.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.5.1 Periodic adjustment caps, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: The increase in the interest that was not imposed because of the rate cap might carry over to future rate adjustments. This is called carryover.

notes.front: What is the side effect of a payment cap that limits a rising ARM payment?
notes.back: It can add to the amount owed: unpaid interest is added to the balance, which is negative amortisation.
notes.explanation: The cap limits the payment, not the interest, so interest not covered is deferred.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 3.6 Payment caps, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: A payment cap can limit the increase to your monthly payments but also can add to the amount you owe on the loan. This is called negative amortization

notes.front: On a loan that caps negative amortisation, what total balance does the cap typically allow, and what happens when it is reached?
notes.back: 110% to 125% of the original loan amount; payments are then reset to repay the loan over the remaining term.
notes.explanation: At that point the payment cap no longer applies, so payments can be much higher.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.3 Negative amortization, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: total amount you can owe to 110 percent to 125 percent of the original loan amount. When you reach that point, the lender will set the monthly payment amounts to fully repay the loan over the remaining term.

notes.front: A first-time borrower is considering a loan that can have negative amortisation. What must the lender make sure of before lending?
notes.back: That the borrower gets homeownership counselling first.
notes.explanation: The handbook states this as a requirement tied to negative amortisation for first-time borrowers.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.3 Negative amortization, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: if you are a first-time borrower, your lender is required to make sure you get homeownership counseling before the lender can lend you the money.

notes.front: A borrower's monthly interest due is $1,150, but the minimum payment chosen is $980, paid on time every month. What happens to the balance?
notes.back: It grows by the unpaid $170 each month: negative amortisation.
notes.explanation: The interest not covered by the payment is added to the loan balance.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.3 Payment-option ARMs, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The unpaid interest is added to the amount you owe on the mortgage, and your loan balance increases. This is called negative amortization.

notes.front: On a payment-option ARM, which of the payment choices may be less than the interest due that month?
notes.back: The minimum (or limited) payment.
notes.explanation: The other options are a full principal-and-interest payment and an interest-only payment.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.3 Payment-option ARMs, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: A minimum (or limited) payment, which may be less than the amount of interest due that month and may not reduce the amount you owe on your mortgage.

notes.front: In a hybrid ARM advertised as 5/1, what do the two numbers mean?
notes.back: Fixed for the first 5 years; after that the rate may adjust every 1 year.
notes.explanation: The first number is the fixed period and the second is how often the rate adjusts afterwards.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.1 Hybrid ARMs, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: the second number tells you how often the rate will adjust after the initial period.

notes.front: A borrower takes a 10/1 hybrid ARM. In which year can the rate first adjust, and how often after that?
notes.back: In year 11, and then once a year.
notes.explanation: The rate is fixed for the first ten years, then adjusts once each year.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), Appendix A: Defined terms, "Hybrid ARM", PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: a 3/1 loan has a fixed rate for the first 3 years and then the rate adjusts once each year beginning in year 4.

notes.front: Why does the payment on an interest-only loan rise when the interest-only period ends, even if rates stay the same?
notes.back: The borrower must start repaying principal as well as interest each month.
notes.explanation: For some interest-only loans the rate also adjusts during the interest-only period.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.2 Interest-only ARMs, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: your monthly payment will increase—even if interest rates stay the same—because you must start paying back the principal as well as the interest each month.

notes.front: A 30-year loan has a 10-year interest-only period. Over how many years must the principal then be repaid?
notes.back: 20 years (the remaining term).
notes.explanation: After the interest-only years the borrower pays principal and interest over the rest of the term.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 4.2 Interest-only ARMs, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: you can pay only interest for five years and then you must pay both the principal and interest over the next 25 years.

notes.front: When a mortgage payment rises sharply at a rate adjustment, the borrower may suffer {{c1::payment shock}}.
notes.explanation: The handbook says it can also happen when an interest-only period ends or a payment-option loan is recast.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.2 Payment shock, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: Payment shock may occur if your mortgage payment rises sharply at a rate adjustment.

notes.front: May an ARM carry a prepayment penalty?
notes.back: No. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau handbook says prepayment penalties are not allowed on ARMs.
notes.explanation: Its glossary adds that they are also not allowed for high-cost mortgages.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.4.1 Prepayment penalties, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: These are called prepayment penalties, and they are not allowed on ARMs.

notes.front: What does a conversion clause in an ARM let the borrower do?
notes.back: Convert the ARM to a fixed-rate mortgage at designated times.
notes.explanation: A convertible ARM may carry higher rates or fees, and a fee at the time of conversion.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.4.2 Conversion fees, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: Your agreement with the lender may include a clause that lets you convert the ARM to a

notes.front: A fixed-rate loan charges one rate for two years, then a set higher rate for the rest of the term. Is it an ARM?
notes.back: No. It is a graduated-payment or stepped-rate loan, not an ARM, though the payment rises as the contract sets.
notes.explanation: The rate change is fixed in the contract rather than tied to an index.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.5 Graduated-payment or stepped-rate loans, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Some fixed-rate loans start with one rate for one or two years and then change to another rate for the remaining term of the loan. While these are not ARMs

notes.front: A borrower plans to stay in the home for decades and wants a principal-and-interest payment that can never change. Which product fits: a 5/1 hybrid ARM or a fixed-rate mortgage?
notes.back: A fixed-rate mortgage.
notes.explanation: Only with a fixed-rate mortgage do the rate and the principal-and-interest payment stay the same for the whole life of the loan.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 2. What is an ARM?, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: with a fixed-rate mortgage, the interest rate and the monthly payment of principal and interest stay the same during the life of the loan.

notes.front: Can the annual percentage rate of an ARM be compared directly with the annual percentage rate of a fixed-rate mortgage?
notes.back: No. Annual percentage rates on similar ARMs can be compared with each other, but not directly with fixed-rate ones, because the ARM rate can change.
notes.explanation: The handbook suggests comparing like with like, for example a 5/1 with a 3/1 ARM.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 6.1 Disclosures from lenders, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: because the interest rate for an ARM can change, APRs on ARMs cannot be compared directly to APRs for fixed-rate mortgages.

notes.front: In a buydown, who typically pays the lender, and what does the borrower get?
notes.back: The seller pays the lender, and the borrower gets a lower rate and payments, usually for an initial period.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns that the seller may raise the sale price to cover the cost.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 5.1 Discounted interest rates, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: This is when the house seller pays an amount to the lender so the lender can give you a lower rate and lower payments, usually for an initial period in an ARM. The seller may increase the sales price to cover the cost of the buydown.

notes.front: How large is a balloon payment generally, relative to the loan's average monthly payment?
notes.back: Generally more than two times the average monthly payment, and often a significant share of the whole loan.
notes.explanation: That size is why the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau calls these loans risky.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a balloon payment? When is one allowed?
notes.evidence: A balloon payment is generally more than two times the loan’s average monthly payment and can often be a significant portion of your entire loan amount.

notes.front: Are balloon payments allowed in a qualified mortgage?
notes.back: Generally no, with some limited exceptions.
notes.explanation: Balloon-payment features are among the features excluded from most qualified mortgage categories.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a balloon payment? When is one allowed?
notes.evidence: balloon payments are not allowed in loans deemed a “ [/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-qualified-mortgage-en-1789/] Qualified Mortgage”, with some limited exceptions.

notes.front: A borrower plans to refinance before a balloon falls due, but the home's value drops sharply. What is the risk?
notes.back: The borrower may not be able to refinance, and could lose the home if the balloon cannot be paid.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes refinancing may fail if the property value falls or the borrower's finances decline.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a balloon payment? When is one allowed?
notes.evidence: However, if the value of your property falls, or if your financial condition declines, you might not be able to do so.

notes.front: Under the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act's definition, is a 15-year fixed-rate mortgage a nontraditional mortgage product?
notes.back: Yes. Anything other than a 30-year fixed rate mortgage is nontraditional under that definition.
notes.explanation: The definition turns on product type alone, not on risk.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. 5102 (SAFE Act definitions), § 5102(7)
notes.evidence: The term "nontraditional mortgage product" means any mortgage product other than a 30-year fixed rate mortgage.
uses: Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act

notes.front: Which mortgage products prompted the 2006 interagency nontraditional mortgage guidance?
notes.back: Products that allow borrowers to defer payment of principal and, sometimes, interest.
notes.explanation: The agencies named interest-only loans and payment-option ARMs as examples.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), I. Background, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: products that allow borrowers to defer

notes.front: In the 2006 nontraditional guidance, what is risk layering?
notes.back: Combining nontraditional features, such as an interest-only loan with reduced documentation or a simultaneous second lien.
notes.explanation: The guidance says an institution that layers features should show mitigating factors support the decision.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), Risk Layering, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: such as interest only loans with reduced

notes.front: Under the 2006 nontraditional guidance, when should stated income be accepted?
notes.back: Only if mitigating factors clearly minimise the need for direct verification of repayment capacity.
notes.explanation: The guidance says reduced documentation substitutes assumptions for analysis and should be used with caution.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), Reduced Documentation, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: accepted only if there are mitigating

notes.front: According to the 2006 guidance, what do simultaneous second-lien loans do to owner equity and credit risk?
notes.back: They reduce owner equity and increase credit risk.
notes.explanation: The guidance adds that, historically, defaults rise as combined loan-to-value ratios rise.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), Simultaneous Second-Lien Loans, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: owner equity and increase credit risk.

notes.front: A lender approves an interest-only loan on stated income, alongside a simultaneous second-lien loan. What does the 2006 guidance call this combination?
notes.back: Risk layering: combining nontraditional features, which increases risk.
notes.explanation: The guidance expects the institution to show that mitigating factors support the decision when features are layered.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), Risk Layering, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: such as interest only loans with reduced

notes.front: What does the 2006 guidance say lenders should recognise about risk-layering features in loans to subprime borrowers?
notes.back: That they may significantly increase risks for both the institution and the borrower.
notes.explanation: The guidance points lenders to the separate interagency subprime guidance, which covers when subprime lending can become predatory or abusive.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), Lending to Subprime Borrowers, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: risks for both the institution and the

notes.front: What are three loan features a General qualified mortgage may not have?
notes.back: Negative amortisation, interest-only features and balloon-payment features (also terms over 30 years).
notes.explanation: A loan with any of them falls outside the General definition, so it would be a non-QM unless another category applies.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.3.2, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: may not have negative-amortization, interest-only features, balloon-payment features, terms that exceed 30 years, or points and fees that exceed the specified limits

notes.front: A creditor offers a fully documented 40-year fixed-rate loan. Can it be a General qualified mortgage?
notes.back: No. General QMs may not have terms over 30 years, so it would be a non-QM.
notes.explanation: The term limit alone rules it out, however strong the borrower.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.3.2, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: may not have negative-amortization, interest-only features, balloon-payment features, terms that exceed 30 years, or points and fees that exceed the specified limits

notes.front: For a first-lien jumbo loan, by how much must the annual percentage rate exceed the average prime offer rate for it to be a higher-priced mortgage loan?
notes.back: By 2.5 or more percentage points (1.5 for a non-jumbo first lien).
notes.explanation: Regulation Z gives jumbo loans a separate, higher threshold.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.35 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.35(a)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: By 2.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a first lien with a principal obligation at consummation that exceeds the limit

notes.front: A first-lien loan above the Freddie Mac purchase limit has an annual percentage rate 2.1 points over the average prime offer rate. Is it a higher-priced mortgage loan?
notes.back: No. As a jumbo loan its threshold is 2.5 points.
notes.explanation: At 2.1 points a non-jumbo first lien would qualify (1.5 threshold), but a jumbo loan does not.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.35 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.35(a)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: By 2.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a first lien with a principal obligation at consummation that exceeds the limit

notes.front: How does a conforming loan differ from a jumbo loan?
notes.back: A conforming loan is at or under the conforming loan limit; a jumbo loan's principal exceeds the Freddie Mac purchase limit.
notes.explanation: Both turn on the same federally set maximum principal for the secondary market.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.35 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, comment 35(a)(1)-3
notes.evidence: when the principal balance exceeds the limit in effect as of the date the transaction's rate is set for the maximum principal obligation eligible for purchase by Freddie Mac (a “jumbo” loan)

notes.front: Besides the usual feature limits, what did a loan need to be a Temporary GSE qualified mortgage?
notes.back: To be eligible for purchase or guarantee by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac while under federal conservatorship.
notes.explanation: This temporary category was tied to the GSEs' conservatorship.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.5.1, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: Additionally, a loan must be eligible for purchase or guarantee by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac while operating under federal conservatorship.

notes.front: On the Loan Estimate, which loan type is disclosed for a loan not guaranteed or insured by any federal or state agency?
notes.back: "Conventional".
notes.explanation: Loan type separates conventional loans from FHA, VA and other government-backed loans.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.37 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.37(a)(11)(i)
notes.evidence: If the loan is not guaranteed or insured by a Federal or State government agency, the creditor shall disclose that the loan is a “Conventional.”

notes.front: A loan is insured by the Federal Housing Administration. Which loan type goes on the Loan Estimate?
notes.back: "FHA".
notes.explanation: Regulation Z gives FHA-insured loans their own loan-type label, separate from conventional and VA loans.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.37 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.37(a)(11)(ii)
notes.evidence: If the loan is insured by the Federal Housing Administration, the creditor shall disclose that the loan is an “FHA.”

notes.front: A loan is guaranteed under the Department of Agriculture's Rural Housing Service. Which loan type goes on the Loan Estimate?
notes.back: "Other", with a brief description of the loan type.
notes.explanation: Only conventional, FHA and VA have their own labels; other government loans fall under "Other".
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.37 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, comment 37(a)(11)-1
notes.evidence: a loan that is guaranteed or funded by the Federal government under the Rural Housing Service (RHS) of the U.S. Department of Agriculture is required to be disclosed under the subcategory “Other.”

notes.front: According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit, what down payment programme does FHA offer?
notes.back: A 3.5% down payment programme.
notes.explanation: The toolkit lists it among low down payment options, with VA and USDA zero down payment programmes.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 4. Choose the right down payment for you, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: FHA, which offers a 3.5% down payment program

notes.front: A creditor totals points and fees on an FHA loan to test the qualified mortgage limit. Does it count the up-front and annual FHA premiums?
notes.back: No. Government-sponsored premiums such as FHA premiums, VA funding fees and USDA guarantee fees are excluded.
notes.explanation: They remain in the finance charge but are left out of the points-and-fees calculation.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.7, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: Federal or state government-sponsored MIPs. For example, exclude up-front and annual FHA premiums, VA funding fees, and USDA guarantee fees.

notes.front: Besides deciding whether to lend, what may lenders use the LTV to decide about insurance or government backing?
notes.back: Whether to require mortgage insurance or a government-guaranteed or insured loan, such as an FHA loan.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau adds that either may raise upfront and monthly costs.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a loan-to-value ratio and how does it relate to my costs?
notes.evidence: Mortgage lenders may use the LTV to decide whether to lend to you and determine if they will require

notes.front: When can a VA home loan require no down payment?
notes.back: When the sales price does not exceed the appraised value.
notes.explanation: The programme also allows financing up to 100 percent of property value.
notes.source: VA, Purchase and Cash-Out Refinance Home Loans, VA Home Loan Advantages
notes.evidence: No down payment if the sales price doesn't exceed the appraised value

notes.front: May the lender on a VA home loan charge a penalty if the borrower pays the loan off early?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The VA lists this among the advantages of the programme.
notes.source: VA, Purchase and Cash-Out Refinance Home Loans, VA Home Loan Advantages
notes.evidence: The lender cannot charge you a penalty fee if you pay the loan off early

notes.front: A veteran selling a home wants the buyer to take over the VA-guaranteed loan. Is that possible, and on what condition?
notes.back: Yes: VA-guaranteed loans are assumable, provided the person assuming the loan qualifies.
notes.explanation: This makes VA loans an example of assumable loans.
notes.source: VA, Purchase and Cash-Out Refinance Home Loans, You should also know that
notes.evidence: VA-guaranteed loans are assumable, as long as the person assuming the loan qualifies.

notes.front: A veteran who already used the VA benefit wants to use remaining entitlement to buy a house to rent out, not to live in. Does the programme allow it?
notes.back: No. With remaining or restored entitlement, the home must be the veteran's residence, as on first use.
notes.explanation: The purchase programme is for homes owned and occupied by the veteran or an eligible dependant.
notes.source: VA, Purchase and Cash-Out Refinance Home Loans, Remaining Entitlement
notes.evidence: you are required to make this home your residence when purchasing a home with remaining or restored entitlement.

notes.front: A company sends monthly payments to a homeowner under a Home Equity Conversion Mortgage. Is that part of servicing under Regulation X?
notes.back: Yes. For a HECM, servicing includes making payments to the borrower.
notes.explanation: In a reverse mortgage money flows to the borrower, so servicing covers those payments.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Servicing"
notes.evidence: In the case of a home equity conversion mortgage or reverse mortgage as referenced in this section, servicing includes making payments to the borrower.

notes.front: How long does a borrower have to rescind a HELOC, and when is there no right to rescind?
notes.back: Three days after a proper rescission notice; no right if the HELOC is used to buy the home.
notes.explanation: The toolkit states the Truth in Lending Act gives this right for HELOCs and refinances.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 4. Understand HELOCs and refinancing, PDF p. 27
notes.evidence: But you can only rescind a refinance or HELOC within three days of receiving a proper notice of the right to rescind from your lender. You cannot rescind if you are using your HELOC to buy a home.

notes.front: A homeowner wants a HELOC to clear large credit card balances run up by ongoing overspending. What caution does the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit give?
notes.back: Using a HELOC as a quick fix for a spending problem could lead back into debt and loss of the home.
notes.explanation: The toolkit reports that financial counsellors caution against using a HELOC this way.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 4. Understand HELOCs and refinancing, PDF p. 27
notes.evidence: If you use a HELOC as a quick fix to a serious spending problem, you could end up back in debt and lose your home.

notes.front: Is a HELOC subject to the ability-to-repay and qualified mortgage rule's ability-to-repay requirements?
notes.back: No. HELOCs, like reverse mortgages and short bridge loans, are not subject to it.
notes.explanation: The guide lists them when describing which loans a small creditor does not count.
notes.source: ATR/QM Rule Small Entity Compliance Guide v3.1 (CFPB, 2021), 4.6, PDF p. 41
notes.evidence: mortgage loans that are not subject to the ATR/QM Rule, such as HELOCs, time-share plans, reverse mortgages, or temporary or bridge loans with terms of 12 months or less.

notes.front: How is the money from a construction loan typically provided?
notes.back: In a series of advances as construction progresses.
notes.explanation: Construction loans also generally carry higher rates than longer-term purchase mortgages.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a construction loan?
notes.evidence: The money borrowed through a construction loan is typically provided in a series of advances as the construction progresses.

notes.front: A construction loan does not automatically convert to a permanent mortgage. What may the borrower have to do at the end?
notes.back: Pay off the balance in a lump sum or reapply for a new loan.
notes.explanation: If the loan does not convert automatically, a new application may be needed.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a construction loan?
notes.evidence: You can pay off the balance in a lump sum or you may be able to convert the loan to a conventional mortgage loan, though if your construction loan does not automatically convert you may have to reapply for a new loan.

notes.front: Is temporary financing such as a construction loan a federally related mortgage loan under Regulation X?
notes.back: Generally no: the definition covers loans other than temporary financing such as construction loans.
notes.explanation: Regulation X carves temporary financing out of the definition.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Federally related mortgage loan"
notes.evidence: Any loan (other than temporary financing, such as a construction loan)

notes.front: A closed-end second-lien loan on a principal dwelling has an annual percentage rate 3.0 points above the average prime offer rate. Is it a higher-priced mortgage loan?
notes.back: No. For subordinate liens the threshold is 3.5 points or more.
notes.explanation: Subordinate-lien loans have the highest of the three thresholds.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.35 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.35(a)(1)(iii)
notes.evidence: By 3.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a subordinate lien.

notes.front: When a creditor knows a piggy-back second mortgage will be made with a first mortgage, must it count that payment in the ability-to-repay review?
notes.back: Yes. It must consider the monthly payment on any simultaneous loan it knows or has reason to know of.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z lists this as one of the factors in the repayment ability determination.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.43 (Regulation Z), CFPB eRegulations, § 1026.43(c)(2)(iv)
notes.evidence: The consumer's monthly payment on any simultaneous loan that the creditor knows or has reason to know will be made

notes.front: In a table-funded loan closed by a mortgage broker in its own name, who is the lender under Regulation X?
notes.back: The person to whom the obligation is initially assigned at or after settlement.
notes.explanation: The lender is the party whose funds are advanced, not the broker named at closing.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Lender"
notes.evidence: the lender is the person to whom the obligation is initially assigned at or after settlement.

notes.front: Is a table-funded transaction a secondary market transaction under Regulation X?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The loan is funded and assigned at settlement itself, so Regulation X does not treat it as a later sale.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1024.2 (Regulation X), CFPB eRegulations, § 1024.2(b), "Table funding"
notes.evidence: A table-funded transaction is not a secondary market transaction

notes.front: When can paying points be a good choice for a borrower?
notes.back: When the borrower plans to keep the loan for a long time.
notes.explanation: Points cost more up front but lower the rate, so the saving builds over time.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: Points can be a good choice if you plan to keep your loan for a long time.

notes.front: Where do points appear on the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure, and what must they be connected to?
notes.back: Page 2, Section A; by law they must be connected to a discounted interest rate.
notes.explanation: This stops a lender calling an ordinary fee "points" on the forms without a rate reduction.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: Points are listed on your [/owning-a-home/loan-estimate/] Loan Estimate and on your [/owning-a-home/closing-disclosure/] Closing Disclosure on page 2, Section A. By law, points listed on your Loan Estimate and on your Closing Disclosure must be connected to a discounted interest rate.

notes.front: On a lender's worksheet, lender credits might be called {{c1::"negative points"}}.
notes.explanation: They are calculated the same way as points, but reduce closing costs instead of the rate.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: Lender credits are calculated the same way as points. They might be called “negative points” on a lender’s worksheet.

notes.front: How do discount points and lender credits trade off cost now against cost over time?
notes.back: Points: pay more at closing for a lower rate. Lender credits: pay less at closing for a higher rate.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes lender credits as working the same way as points, in reverse.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: Lender credits work the same way as points, in reverse. You pay a higher interest rate and the lender gives you money to offset your closing costs.

notes.front: A buyer has little cash for closing but can afford a larger monthly payment. Which option fits: points or lender credits?
notes.back: Lender credits: a higher rate in exchange for money toward closing costs.
notes.explanation: Paying less up front means paying more over time through the higher rate.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: How should I use lender credits and points (also called discount points)?
notes.evidence: When you receive lender credits, you pay less up front, but you pay more over time because the interest rate is higher.

notes.front: How does the size of the down payment affect the LTV?
notes.back: The higher the down payment, the lower the LTV.
notes.explanation: A bigger down payment means less is financed against the same appraised value.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a loan-to-value ratio and how does it relate to my costs?
notes.evidence: The higher your down payment, the lower your LTV ratio.

notes.front: What interest rate are borrowers with a higher LTV usually offered?
notes.back: A higher interest rate, as higher-risk borrowers.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes a larger down payment may earn a better rate.
notes.source: Ask CFPB: What is a loan-to-value ratio and how does it relate to my costs?
notes.evidence: Higher-risk borrowers, those with a higher LTV, will usually be offered a higher interest rate.
